sections.text:
Division asks a question: **how many groups of this size fit?** 3 ÷ 1/4 asks, "How many 1/4s fit in 3?"

Look at 3 wholes, each cut into 4 parts. Count the parts: 3 × 4 = **12**.

Here is the shortcut: **keep, change, flip.** Keep the first number, change ÷ to ×, and flip the second number.

3 ÷ 1/4 → 3 × 4/1 = 12. Same answer as counting!
Why does flipping work? Each whole holds 4 quarters, so multiplying by 4 counts all of them at once. When the answer isn't whole, part of a group is left over. That's OK!

learn.keyIdea: Dividing by a fraction = multiplying by its reciprocal (keep, change, flip).

examples.title: Counting quarters

steps.do: Draw 3 whole bars and cut each into 4 equal parts.
steps.why: Each part is 1/4, so the question becomes counting parts.

steps.do: Count: 4 parts in each whole, and there are 3 wholes, so 3 × 4 = 12.
steps.why: Multiplying is a fast way to count equal groups.
Flipping 1/4 to 4/1 is just the shortcut for 'how many quarters in each whole'.

examples.mistake: Don't flip the first number! Only flip the number you are dividing by.

steps.do: Draw a number line from 0 to 1 marked in eighths.
steps.why: Eighths are the size of each jump we want to count.

steps.do: On the line from 0 to 1, jump by 1/8 from 0 to 3/4 and count the jumps: 6.
steps.why: 3/4 is the same as 6/8, so six 1/8-jumps land exactly on it.
The shortcut and the jumps must agree.

examples.title: When it doesn't fit evenly

steps.do: Rename both with a common denominator: 3/4 = 9/12 and 2/3 = 8/12.
steps.why: Same-size pieces make them easy to compare.

steps.do: Ask: how many groups of 8 twelfths fit in 9 twelfths? 9 ÷ 8 = 9/8.
steps.why: One full group fits, plus 1/8 of another group.
Both ways give the same answer, so the shortcut works.

examples.mistake: An answer bigger than 1 is fine here: 2/3 fits into 3/4 a bit more than once.

examples.title: Snack bags
examples.prompt: Andrew has 4 cups of trail mix. Each bag holds 2/3 cup. How many bags can he fill?

steps.why: We want to know how many 2/3-cup groups fit in 4 cups.

steps.do: Each cup has 3 thirds, so 4 cups have 12 thirds. Each bag uses 2 thirds: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
steps.why: Counting thirds shows the reasoning behind the shortcut.
The shortcut gives the same 6 bags.

steps.hint: Swap the top and bottom of 1/3.

steps.hint: Multiply tops together and bottoms together, then simplify.

sections.text: Long division splits a big number into equal groups **one place value at a time**. In 864, we share the 8 hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones.
Repeat four moves: **Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down.** A silly way to remember: *Does McDonald's Sell Burgers?* 🍔
Always check by multiplying: quotient × divisor should give you the number you started with.

learn.keyIdea: Divide → Multiply → Subtract → Bring down, then check by multiplying.

examples.title: Sharing by place value

steps.do: How many 4s fit in 8? 2. Write 2, multiply 2 × 4 = 8, subtract: 8 − 8 = 0.
steps.why: We split the big number one place value at a time, starting with the biggest place.

steps.do: Bring down the next digit to make 6. How many 4s fit in 6? 1. Write 1, multiply 1 × 4 = 4, subtract: 6 − 4 = 2.
steps.why: We split the big number one place value at a time, starting with the biggest place.

steps.do: Bring down the next digit to make 24. How many 4s fit in 24? 6. Write 6, multiply 6 × 4 = 24, subtract: 24 − 24 = 0.
steps.why: We split the big number one place value at a time, starting with the biggest place.
Each digit came from one place value: 2 hundreds, 1 ten, 6 ones.

examples.mistake: After subtracting, always bring down the next digit before dividing again.

examples.title: Two-digit divisor

steps.do: 24 does not fit in 1 or 15, so start with 151.
steps.why: We need a number at least as big as 24 to make a group.

steps.do: How many 24s fit in 151? 6. Write 6, multiply 6 × 24 = 144, subtract: 151 − 144 = 7.
steps.why: We split the big number one place value at a time, starting with the biggest place.

steps.do: Bring down the next digit to make 72. How many 24s fit in 72? 3. Write 3, multiply 3 × 24 = 72, subtract: 72 − 72 = 0.
steps.why: We split the big number one place value at a time, starting with the biggest place.
6 tens and 3 ones make 63.

examples.mistake: Estimate first: 24 is about 25, and 1,500 ÷ 25 = 60, so 63 makes sense.

When 35 fits 0 times, we still write a 0 to hold that place.

sections.text: Every digit has a place. In 16.25, the 2 means 2 tenths and the 5 means 5 hundredths.
**Add and subtract:** line up the decimal points so tenths add to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.
**Multiply:** 0.3 × 0.4 means 3 tenths of 4 tenths. On a 10-by-10 grid, the overlap is 12 little squares out of 100, which is 0.12.
**Divide:** move the decimal point in both numbers the same number of places until you divide by a whole number.

learn.keyIdea: Line up decimals to add/subtract; count decimal places to multiply; make the divisor whole to divide.

steps.why: Tenths must add to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.

examples.mistake: Don't line up the last digits — line up the decimal points!

steps.why: Each row or column is one tenth of the whole square.
The overlap shows 0.3 of 0.4.

steps.do: Each small square is 1/100, so 12 squares = 0.12.
steps.why: There are 100 small squares in the whole grid.

examples.check: 0.12 is less than both 0.3 and 0.4, which makes sense when multiplying numbers less than 1. ✅

sections.text: The **greatest common factor (GCF)** is the biggest number that divides two numbers evenly. The GCF of 18 and 24 is 6.
The GCF helps you rewrite sums. 24 + 36 = 12 × 2 + 12 × 3 = **12(2 + 3)**. Picture a rectangle 12 tall, split into a 2-wide part and a 3-wide part.
The **least common multiple (LCM)** is the smallest number both numbers divide into. Count by 6s (6, 12, 18, 24) and by 8s (8, 16, 24): they first meet at **24**.

learn.keyIdea: GCF = biggest shared factor (splitting); LCM = smallest shared multiple (meeting up).

examples.title: Finding a GCF

steps.why: Factors are numbers that divide evenly.
We need both lists to find the shared ones.
GCF means the greatest common one.
steps.rule: GCF = largest factor in both lists

examples.check: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4, and 3 and 4 share no factor except 1. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't pick the smallest shared factor — pick the greatest!

examples.title: Meeting up with an LCM

We're looking for the first number on both lists.

steps.why: That makes it the least common multiple.
steps.rule: LCM = smallest number in both multiple lists

examples.mistake: 6 × 8 = 48 is a common multiple, but not the least one.

steps.why: 10 is the biggest number that divides both.
Pulling out the 10 shows what's left in each part.
The distributive property lets us undo multiplying 10 by each part.

steps.why: The GCF is the biggest shared factor.
steps.worked: Shared factors are 1, 2, 3, 6; the greatest is 6.

steps.why: The LCM is the first place the two skip-counts meet.

sections.text: Numbers can go **below zero**! Temperatures below 0, money you owe, and depths below sea level are **negative**. On this line, −8 is 8 steps left of 0 and 8 is 8 steps right.
**Opposites** are the same distance from 0 but on different sides, like 8 and −8.
The opposite of an opposite is the number you started with: −(−3) = 3. Two flips bring you back! 🔁

learn.keyIdea: Negative = below zero; opposites mirror each other across 0.

examples.title: Below sea level
examples.prompt: Write an integer for "20 feet below sea level".

steps.why: We measure up and down from sea level.
Numbers below 0 are negative.

examples.check: −20 is 20 units from 0 on the negative side. ✅
examples.mistake: Don't drop the negative sign — 20 would mean 20 feet above sea level.

steps.why: Distance from 0 tells us how far to go on the other side.
Opposites are mirror images across 0.

examples.title: Double opposite

steps.why: The minus sign means 'the opposite of'.
Flipping across 0 twice brings you back to the start.

examples.check: 3 and −3 are opposites, so −(−3) must be 3. ✅
examples.mistake: Two negatives here don't make −3 — the opposite of a negative is positive.

sections.text: **Absolute value** is distance from 0. Distance is never negative, so |−12| = 12 and |12| = 12.
To **compare**, picture a number line. Numbers to the **right are greater**. So −1 > −3.5, even though 3.5 is bigger than 1!
Absolute value is useful for size: a debt of −$45 is a **bigger debt** than −$30 because |−45| = 45 > 30.

learn.keyIdea: |x| = distance from 0; on a number line, right is greater.

examples.title: Distance from zero

steps.why: Absolute value measures how far a number is from 0.
Distance doesn't care about direction.

examples.check: 12 is also |12|, the same distance on the other side. ✅

steps.why: A number line shows order clearly.

steps.do: −1 is to the right of −3.5, so −1 > −3.5.
steps.why: Numbers get greater as you move right.

examples.mistake: Don't compare just the digits — with negatives, the one farther from 0 is smaller.

steps.why: Seeing them on a line makes order easy.
Left to right is least to greatest.

examples.prompt: Account A has a balance of −$30. Account B has −$45. Which shows a bigger debt?

steps.why: The size of a debt is how far below 0 the balance is.

steps.do: 45 > 30, so Account B owes more; on the line, −45 is farther left of 0 than −30.
steps.why: A bigger absolute value means a bigger debt.

examples.check: Even though −45 < −30, the debt of $45 is bigger. ✅

sections.text: A point (x, y) is like directions: move **x** left or right first, then **y** up or down. (−3, 4) means 3 left, 4 up.
The axes split the plane into four **quadrants**, numbered I, II, III, IV counterclockwise, starting at the top right.

**Reflecting** across an axis flips one sign. Across the x-axis, flip y. Across the y-axis, flip x.

To find the **distance** between points in the same row or column, count the units between them.

learn.keyIdea: (x, y): across, then up; reflect = flip one sign; same row/column → count the gap.

examples.title: Which quadrant?

steps.why: Negative x means left of the y-axis.

steps.do: y = 4 is positive, so go up.
steps.why: Positive y means above the x-axis.

steps.do: Left and up is Quadrant II.

steps.rule: Opposite sides: add the absolute values

steps.why: Adding the two parts gives the whole distance.
